brief: The layers under a decision, and which one people actually argue about

slots.eyebrow: On what people are really arguing about
slots.subtitle: Six things about where a disagreement actually lives, and why the argument almost never happens there.
slots.v1: The top layer, where everybody can see it.
slots.v2: One or two layers down, usually without a meeting.
slots.coverNote: The last page is the case where the top layer is the point

slots.body: Almost every meeting is spent on the top layer — the wording, the colour, the name — because it is the only one everybody can see and therefore the only one everybody can have an opinion about.
slots.v1: Where the discussion happens, and where the least is at stake.
slots.v2: Where the decision was actually made, usually silently.
slots.v3: Where it was made for you, before anybody sat down.

slots.body: By the time you are choosing words, the shape has already ruled out most of them. Arguing about the top layer when you dislike the one beneath it is how a project spends six weeks going nowhere pleasantly.
slots.v1: Cheap to change, and it changes nothing.
slots.v2: Expensive to change, and it changes everything.
slots.v3: Not yours to change at all this quarter.

slots.body: Budget, timeline, platform, the thing that shipped two years ago. These are not up for discussion in the room you are in, and pretending otherwise is the most common way a team wastes a month.
slots.v1: Where you have authority and almost no leverage.
slots.v2: Where you have some of both, if you ask early.
slots.v3: Where you have leverage only by escalating.

slots.body: Leverage is highest at the bottom and permission is lowest. The useful question is not what would be best, it is which is the deepest layer somebody in this room is allowed to change, and then to spend the effort there.
slots.v1: Explicitly, at the start. Most of it is assumed, not decided.
slots.v2: From wording to shape. From shape to premise.
slots.v3: Recognising it early is worth more than being right about it.

slots.body: The rewrite that does not help, the redesign that changes nothing, the rename. Each one is an attempt to solve a lower layer from the top, and it fails in the same way every time — it looks different and behaves identically.
slots.v1: Keeps coming back after each fix. That is the tell.
slots.v2: Sits one or two layers down from where you are working.
slots.v3: If it recurs, you fixed the wrong layer.

slots.body: Not every problem is deep, and treating every request as a symptom of something structural is its own way of avoiding work. Some things genuinely just need the wording fixed, and diagnosing it as profound is a way of not doing it.
slots.v1: Is there a layer under this? Then accept the answer.
slots.v2: Most requests are exactly what they appear to be.
slots.v3: For the problem that has come back three times.

slots.eyebrow: At the start of the next disagreement
slots.body: One question, asked out loud in the first five minutes: which parts of this are actually still open. Most of the room is assuming a different answer.
slots.closingLine: You cannot win an argument on a layer nobody in the room is allowed to change.
slots.signoff: Leverage is lowest where permission is highest
